In summary, our research is concerned with
the source and H2O contents of high-Mg basalts in island arc settings.
the question: how much water is required to produce the observed range of arc magma compositions and what is the source of the water?
the question whether high-MgO arc basalts are primary melts or whether they are the result of fractional crystallization processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the source of arc magmas is heterogeneous and variable in its water content.
the high-MgO STV301 is a product of partial mantle melting, but the mantle source of STV301 is not dry and may contain up to ~0.3 wt % H2O.
high-MgO melts in island arc settings may be extracted from the mantle under both dry and hydrous conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the STV301 basalt was extracted from a lherzolotic mantle source under oxidizing conditions, at 0.3-1.5 wt.% H2O, and at a depth of 60-70 km.
the H2O concentration in the mantle source is a critical control on the degree of melting, but that the H2 O concentration of the extracted melt is a function of the degree of melting.
the H2O content in the mantle source of arc magmas is not a major controlling factor on the liquidus phase relations of the primary magmas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the H2O concentration in the melt at the time of its extraction from the mantle is not a good proxy for the degree of melting.
the H2O content in the source is a major control on the degree of melting of the mantle wedge and, therefore, on the composition of the extracted melts.

the high-MgO basalts of the Lesser Antilles arc are not the result of melting of a hydrous peridotite source, but are rather a product of melting of a lherzolites source with a low initial H2O content.
